summary: A 1977 specification for the Network Voice Protocol, an early scheme for sending digitised speech over a packet network. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: The Network Voice Protocol (NVP) separates call setup from voice data so two systems can negotiate compatible voice settings before exchanging speech. Voice data is sent in parcels with timing information.

subtitle: A protocol for negotiating and carrying real-time voice over the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET's host-to-host protocol was designed for data transfer and was unsuitable for real-time interactive voice communication.
tldr.mechanism: NVP separates call control and codec negotiation from voice data, using separate directional links and voice parcels with timing information.
tldr.outcome: The RFC says NVP was first implemented in December 1973 and used for local and transnet voice communication at several listed sites; the unit metadata records its status as Unknown.

facts.label: Control and data links per call

today: The unit metadata records RFC 741's status as Unknown and lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. The RFC describes the Network Voice Protocol and implementations reported at the time.

sections.title: Voice Communication over a Packet Network
sections.content:
The RFC says the ARPANET was designed for data transfer, but real-time interactive voice needed a different communication discipline. NVP was designed to support voice over the network, recover from lost messages without catastrophic effects, avoid end-to-end retransmission, separate control from data, and adapt to network performance.

The protocol has a control protocol and a data protocol. Control messages set up and negotiate the call; data messages carry encoded speech.
sections.plainLanguage: Voice conversations need low delay, so lost voice data cannot simply be retransmitted later. NVP uses separate rules for setting up a call and sending voice.

sections.title: Call Setup and Negotiation
sections.content:
Each call uses four links: one control and one data link in each direction. The caller starts on link 377 octal, identifies the caller and recipient, and proposes a return control link. The answerer can refuse or accept and assign another link.

The parties then negotiate compatible settings, such as vocoding method, sample period, version and maximum message length. One party acts as negotiation master and proposes options; the other accepts or rejects them. After successful negotiation, the answerer may send RINGING if a person must answer. READY indicates that a party can accept data.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller and answerer first set up separate paths for control and voice in both directions. They agree on voice settings before the call begins sending data.

sections.title: Voice Parcels and Message Timing
sections.content:
Voice data is sent in parcels, each representing a frame for an agreed transmission interval. Network messages contain a whole number of parcels. The first 32 bits of each data message form a header with a time stamp, a skipped-parcels flag and a parcel count.

The specified LPC data protocol uses shared tables to encode speech parameters. The RFC describes simple acoustic coding, which sends all parameters at each interval, and optimized coding, which sends only what is acoustically needed. It defines only the simple acoustic format here and says simple information coding is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The voice stream is divided into parcels, and each message says which parcel it starts with and how many it contains. The receiver can use the timing information to notice gaps.

sections.title: Implementations Described
sections.content:
The acknowledgments say NVP was first implemented in December 1973 and had been used for local and transnet real-time voice communication over the ARPANET. The listed sites are ISI, Lincoln Laboratory, Culler-Harrison and Stanford Research Institute, with implementations using LPC or CVSD as specified for each site.

The RFC includes control-message examples, the definition of Tables-Set-#1 for LPC and implementation recommendations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC reports that several sites had implemented NVP for real-time voice. It lists the sites and the voice-coding methods they used.
